ingredients.name: Kankun (water spinach)
ingredients.notes: leaves and tender stems, washed thoroughly and roughly chopped; Chinese water spinach or morning glory are the same plant; regular spinach can substitute

ingredients.name: Freshly grated coconut
ingredients.notes: about 1 cup; unsweetened desiccated coconut rehydrated in a little warm water works as a substitute

ingredients.name: Coconut oil
ingredients.notes: optional; traditional mallung uses little or no oil

steps.instruction: Wash the kankun thoroughly -- water spinach grows in water and can carry grit and sediment, so rinse in several changes of water. Separate the leaves from the thicker stalks; finely chop the stalks (they take longer to cook) and roughly chop the leaves. Keep them separate.
In a bowl, combine the coconut, shallots, garlic, green chillies, turmeric, chilli flakes (if using), Maldive fish (if using), and salt. Mix together well.
Heat the coconut oil (if using) in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Add the chopped stalks first and stir-fry for 1-2 minutes until they begin to soften.

Add the coconut-spice mixture along with the chopped leaves. Toss everything together over medium-high heat, stirring continuously, for about 3-4 minutes until the leaves are just wilted and the coconut is lightly toasted.
Remove from the heat immediately while the kankun is still bright green -- overcooking turns it dull and slimy. Stir in the lime juice. Taste and adjust salt. Serve warm alongside rice and curry.

source_site: sbs.com.au, cross-checked against islandsmile.org, chhayasfood.com, ankierenique.wordpress.com, grokipedia.com, and Wikipedia (Mallung)
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 6+ independent sources; strong agreement on the quick stir-fry technique and stopping while still bright green
notes: Kankun (Ipomoea aquatica) is a semi-aquatic leafy green widely cultivated in Sri Lanka's wet low-country zones; it is sold in bundles at most local markets. The same plant is called water morning glory, water convolvulus, swamp cabbage, or kangkung across Asia. It has a mild, slightly grassy flavour and wilts very quickly -- 3-4 minutes is typically enough. Like all mallung preparations, the key is to stop cooking while the greens are still bright and retain slight bite; overcooked kankun turns dark, slimy, and unappetising. The plant's hollow stems cook faster than the leaves, so adding them first (as in step 3) ensures even cooking.
